records.sourceFile: Explaining variation in sweat sodium concentration - Effect of individual characteristics and exercise, environmental, and dietary factors.pdf

paper.citation: Baker LB, De Chavez PJD, Nuccio RP, Brown SD, King MA, Sopeña BC, et al. Explaining variation in sweat sodium concentration: effect of individual characteristics and exercise, environmental, and dietary factors. J Appl Physiol. 2022;133:1250-1259.
paper.abstract: In a retrospective analysis of 1,944 whole-body sweat sodium tests from 1,304 athletes and recreational exercisers, stepwise regression explained 17-23% of the variation in sweat sodium concentration. Energy expenditure and season of the year (a proxy for heat acclimatization) were the most important factors, while sex, exercise mode, air temperature and whole-body sweating rate contributed in some models. Age group, race/ethnicity, fluid balance and sodium intake were not associated with sweat sodium.
paper.tldr: Higher energy expenditure was associated with higher whole-body sweat sodium and warm-season testing with lower sweat sodium, but all measured factors together explained only about a fifth of the variation. The authors conclude that predicting sweat sodium without individualized sweat patch testing is difficult.
paper.methods: Retrospective multiple regression (stepwise, P < 0.05 for entry) of sweat tests compiled from Gatorade Sports Science Institute service and research testing from 2000 to 2020. Whole-body sweat sodium was estimated from forearm patches in models 1 and 2 and measured by whole-body washdown in a controlled 90-min cycling subset (model 3, n = 48).
paper.findings: Model 1 (1,944 tests, 1,304 subjects, adjusted R2 0.17) retained warm season, cycling, male sex, whole-body sweating rate and body mass, and model 2 (1,003 tests, 607 subjects, adjusted R2 0.19) retained warm season, energy expenditure, cycling, air temperature and male sex. Warm-season tests were associated with lower sweat sodium, while higher energy expenditure, cycling, male sex and higher air temperature were associated with higher sweat sodium; in the laboratory cycling subset (model 3, unadjusted R2 0.23), energy expenditure was the only significant predictor. Age group, race/ethnicity, relative humidity, exercise duration, urine specific gravity, fluid balance, relative VO2max, and dietary or exercise sodium intake were not significant in any model.
paper.limitations: The data are a retrospective convenience sample from one laboratory, with a male-majority sample, and race/ethnicity was dropped from model 2 for limited diversity. Heat acclimatization was estimated only from season, and field energy expenditure came from GPS or accelerometer devices with limited accuracy. The models explained only 17-23% of the variation, and model 3 rests on 48 tests from one controlled protocol.
paper.practicalImplications: Repeat sweat testing when training or competition changes meaningfully in intensity, air temperature, exercise mode or season, because these factors shifted sweat sodium in the models. Athletes with higher energy expenditure had higher sweat sodium, so heavy-output blocks should not be assumed to share one sweat sodium value. Do not use age group, race/ethnicity or fluid balance as a shortcut to estimate sweat sodium, since they were not significant predictors.
paper.athleteDev: Repeat sweat testing when training or competition differs in sweating demand, environment, exercise mode or season, because these factors shifted sweat sodium in the models. Higher energy expenditure was associated with higher sweat sodium, so sessions with high energy output should not be assumed to share one sweat sodium value.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It includes no injured or rehabilitating athletes and does not test any return-to-sport criteria, so it should not be used for those decisions.

paper.citation: Di C, Jia W. Food-derived bioactive peptides as momentous food components: Can functional peptides passed through the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway and NF-κB pathway to repair and protect the skeletal muscle injury? Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition. 2023.
paper.abstract: Skeletal muscle injury from overuse or trauma is common in sport, and the authors review food-derived bioactive peptides as nutritional aids for muscle repair. They summarise the proposed mechanisms (PI3K/Akt/mTOR protein synthesis, oxidative stress, inflammation, cartilage, tendon and connective tissue) and list peptide sources from meat, fish, dairy, egg, plants and fruit.
paper.tldr: Food-derived peptides are proposed to support muscle repair through protein synthesis, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways. Most of this evidence is preclinical, so it is not yet a basis for recovery prescriptions.
paper.methods: Narrative review. No systematic search, selection criteria or risk-of-bias appraisal is described. Evidence is drawn from cell, animal, in vitro and selected human studies.
paper.findings: The authors propose that peptides may act on the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, oxidative stress and NF-κB-linked inflammation after muscle injury. Human examples cited include a 14-week collagen peptide plus resistance training trial in 40 healthy young men (tendon and muscle hypertrophy outcomes) and a crossover study of protein and carbohydrate after exercise in 35 men that reported changes in serum cytokines. The authors state that most peptide research is still at the laboratory stage and call for human studies, yet they also conclude that peptide intake is "a good and safe way to improve the skeletal muscle function", which goes beyond the human evidence they cite.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how studies were searched or selected, so the evidence base cannot be audited. Most mechanistic and peptide data are from cell and rodent work, and the human studies are few and small. The authors list open problems themselves: separation methods for industrial production, possible allergic reactions, and the need for in vivo activity and safety testing.
paper.practicalImplications: Peptide-containing foods or supplements should not be presented to staff as proven recovery aids for injured athletes on the strength of this review. Protein-based nutrition after muscle-damaging exercise is supported in general terms by the human studies cited, and any specific peptide use would need trial-level evidence in athletes.
paper.athleteDev: The review gives no performance training protocol. Its human examples concern exercise-induced muscle damage and training adaptation in healthy or physically active young men, and the authors call for more human data before any performance claim.
paper.rtp: This review cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or nutrition timelines. Its tendon and cartilage examples come from Achilles tendinopathy patients, healthy men and rodent models, and none tests a return-to-play outcome in athletes.

records.sourceFile: Food first but not always food only - Recommendations for using dietary supplements in sport.pdf

paper.citation: Close GL, Kasper AM, Walsh NP, Maughan RJ. 'Food first but not always food only': Recommendations for using dietary supplements in sport. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2022. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Narrative review proposing a working definition of 'food first' as meaning that, where practical, nutrients come from whole foods rather than isolated components or supplements. It sets out six reasons a food-only approach may not be optimal for athletes, including nutrients that are hard to obtain, variable nutrient content of foods and food contamination concerns. It then summarizes evidence for specific supplements and advises that any supplement use be batch tested and risk-managed.
paper.tldr: Food first should mean that nutrients come from whole foods where practical, but it is not always food only. A small set of supplements with good evidence, such as caffeine, creatine, nitrate and beta-alanine, can be justified when food cannot supply the dose, and only if they are batch tested and used with a risk-management plan.
paper.methods: Narrative review in which the authors explore the food first concept and give guidance on delivering it safely. No systematic search, inclusion criteria or evidence grading are described.
paper.findings: The authors propose six criteria for when a food-only approach may not be optimal: nutrients that are hard to obtain in sufficient amounts, nutrients found only in foods athletes avoid, variable nutrient content of foods, high doses needed to correct deficiency or promote tolerance, foods that are hard to eat around exercise, and food hygiene or contamination concerns. For creatine, beta-alanine and nitrate the review states that the required doses are difficult or impractical to reach from food alone, and for caffeine the problem is that the dose in coffee is too variable to control (15 to 254 mg per serving); for sodium bicarbonate, food-based loading would need a high-carbohydrate, low-protein diet that is not optimal for other aspects of performance. For immune health, the authors note that supplements aimed at boosting immune resistance have shown little if any benefit in athletes, but suggest that vitamin D, vitamin C and probiotics may reduce illness during the common cold season and that zinc lozenges taken within 24 hours of onset may shorten a cold, citing meta-analyses and Cochrane reviews that are partly from non-athlete populations.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, so the choice of evidence cannot be checked. Many supporting claims are taken from cited meta-analyses and consensus statements rather than from new analysis. Several immune recommendations rest on general or military population data. The author disclosures list consultancy, honoraria or research funding from sports organizations and nutrition companies, including the Gatorade Sports Science Institute.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat food first as the default, and consider a targeted supplement only when the review's criteria apply, for example when a creatine or nitrate dose cannot realistically come from food or a known caffeine dose is needed. Any supplement should be independently batch tested and used with a risk-management plan, because batch testing reduces but does not remove contamination and labelling risk. Immune supplements such as vitamin D, vitamin C, probiotics or zinc lozenges are framed for specific high-risk scenarios (cold season, foreign travel, onset of a cold), not as routine immune boosters.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports targeted supplements such as creatine, caffeine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate when food cannot supply the required dose, provided they are batch tested and risk-managed. It presents carbohydrate and protein products as practical options around training and competition when whole foods are hard to consume.
paper.rtp: Limited application: the review mentions collagen and iron deficiency in relation to tissue repair and performance, based on the studies it cites. It gives no return-to-sport protocol and cannot guide return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Food for thought - Physiological considerations for nutritional ergogenic.pdf

paper.citation: Wickham KA, Spriet LL. Food for thought: Physiological considerations for nutritional ergogenic efficacy. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2023.
paper.abstract: Brief narrative review of the physiological considerations that determine whether an orally ingested nutritional ergogenic aid can improve athletic performance. The authors discuss first-pass metabolism, rises in systemic concentration and interaction with target tissues, and explore mouth rinsing as a route that bypasses these barriers. They also cover practical factors that alter efficacy, including human variability, dosing, training status, sex differences and placebo effects.
paper.tldr: An orally taken supplement should survive first-pass metabolism, raise circulating levels for a useful period and reach its target tissue, as creatine, beta-alanine and nitrate do. Study designs should control dose, training status, sex, placebo and blinding, because these can change whether an effect appears.
paper.methods: Narrative review in which the authors build a framework of three physiological considerations for oral ergogenic aids and illustrate it with examples. No systematic search or study selection criteria are described.
paper.findings: The authors state that an oral aid is likely to be effective only if it survives first-pass metabolism in sufficient quantities, produces a substantial rise in systemic concentration for a reasonable time, and interacts with or is taken up by the target tissue. Creatine and beta-alanine are presented as raising muscle stores, and dietary nitrate is reported to reduce the oxygen cost of submaximal exercise in recreationally trained males, with benefits described as mostly limited to recreationally active people and stop-and-go team sport athletes rather than elite endurance athletes, and emerging evidence of no benefit in women. Taurine raised plasma levels without changing human muscle taurine or cycling performance, carnitine raised plasma only modestly (about 30%) with no change in muscle content after 14 days, and pyruvate and microhydrin did not rise in the blood or improve performance. Carbohydrate mouth rinsing is described as consistently ergogenic through the central nervous system, while performance effects of caffeine rinsing are mixed.
paper.limitations: The authors state the review is not meant to cover all potential ergogenic aids, and it does not grade the strength of the cited studies. The examples are selected to illustrate the framework, so the review does not give a complete or systematic picture of any one supplement. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
paper.practicalImplications: Before assuming a supplement will help, check whether there is evidence it reaches the target tissue at a useful concentration. Trials should standardize dose, co-ingestion (such as carbohydrate with creatine), training status and blinding, and should not assume an aid that works in recreational athletes will work in elite athletes. Staff should expect the size and direction of a supplement effect to vary with training status, sex and the demands of the sport.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review provides a checklist for judging whether an oral supplement is plausible (first-pass metabolism, circulating rise, target tissue). It notes that benefits can differ by training status, sex and sport, for example nitrate effects appearing more in stop-and-go team sport athletes than in elite endurance athletes. It gives no dosing protocol for staff use.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the review addresses ergogenic efficacy and does not discuss injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Food‑First Approach to Enhance the Regulation of Post‑exercise Skeletal Muscle Protein Synthesis and Remodeling.pdf

paper.citation: Burd NA, Beals JW, Martinez IG, Salvador AF, Skinner SK. Food-First Approach to Enhance the Regulation of Post-exercise Skeletal Muscle Protein Synthesis and Remodeling. Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: Review of protein quality, the food matrix and post-exercise muscle protein synthesis. The authors argue that meal-based protein recommendations are built on isolated proteins, while whole foods contain non-protein components that may modulate the anabolic response. They conclude that a food-first approach is likely beneficial for both muscle adaptation and diet quality, but the food matrix hypothesis still requires rigorous testing.
paper.tldr: The authors argue that whole protein foods, with their other nutrients, may support post-exercise muscle protein synthesis as well as or better than isolated proteins, so a food-first approach is likely beneficial for most people. This remains a hypothesis, because current meal-level protein guidance comes mainly from studies of isolated proteins such as whey and casein.
paper.methods: Narrative review of protein quality scores (PDCAAS and DIAAS), the leucine trigger hypothesis, food matrix effects and exercise-induced gut permeability. No literature search, selection criteria or evidence grading are described, and the review draws on the authors' own studies and cited work.
paper.findings: The authors report that post-exercise MPS plateaus at about 0.25 g protein/kg per meal in healthy young men when isolated protein is consumed, and that whole foods can stimulate MPS despite a slower rise in leucine. In the cited studies, skim milk gave greater MPS than beef during early (0 to 2 h) recovery, and whole eggs gave a greater post-exercise MPS response than an isonitrogenous amount of egg white. The authors also summarize that exercise increases intestinal permeability, which returns to baseline faster when food is consumed afterwards, and suggest this may allow food components to reach the circulation. The authors state that which food components or mechanisms drive the matrix effect is not known.
paper.limitations: No search method is described, so the choice of evidence cannot be checked. The matrix case rests on a few acute MPS comparison studies, and studies that co-ingested casein with single milk components (milk fat, carbohydrate, milk serum) were done at rest and showed no added MPS response, so the authors suggest an exercise stimulus may be needed. The supplement was supported by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute, and the first author reports honoraria from that institute and research support from the National Cattlemen's Beef Association and the Alliance for Potato Research and Education.
paper.practicalImplications: Dietitians should consider an athlete's eating pattern (animal- or plant-based), travel and training schedule when deciding between whole foods and supplements. In the cited studies, whole-food protein sources such as milk and eggs supported a post-exercise MPS response, so they are reasonable choices when they suit the athlete's diet. The advantage of the food matrix over an equivalent isolated protein is not established.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review argues that whole foods such as milk and eggs may support the muscle protein synthesis response to training through components beyond protein. Dietitians should plan post-exercise protein around the athlete's diet and schedule, while treating the matrix advantage as a hypothesis.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the review addresses post-exercise muscle protein synthesis and remodeling in healthy adults and athletes, and does not discuss injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport nutrition. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: From Food Supplements to Functional Foods - Emerging Perspectives on Post-Exercise Recovery Nutrition.pdf

paper.citation: Wang L, Meng Q, Su CH. From Food Supplements to Functional Foods: Emerging Perspectives on Post-Exercise Recovery Nutrition. Nutrients. 2024;16:4081.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers post-exercise recovery nutrition, from traditional supplements (protein, carbohydrate, creatine, BCAAs, electrolytes) to functional foods with bioactive compounds such as tart cherry juice, turmeric, omega-3 sources, and probiotics. The authors searched PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar for English-language studies from 2000 to 2024. They conclude that functional foods and personalized nutrition may support recovery alongside a balanced diet, and that dosage, nutrient interactions and long-term effects need more research.
paper.tldr: Protein, carbohydrate and electrolyte intake are presented as core recovery needs, with dairy, tart cherry and omega-3 foods as complements. The authors note that evidence for BCAAs, bromelain and long-term supplement use is mixed or limited.
paper.methods: Narrative review of PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar searches (English-language, 2000 to 2024) using keyword Boolean combinations. Studies were selected for relevance to recovery outcomes and grouped by theme. The authors describe the quality review as informal, with no structured risk-of-bias assessment.
paper.findings: The review summarizes protein and carbohydrate timing, electrolyte replacement, and functional foods such as dairy, tart cherry juice, turmeric and omega-3 sources. It reports that plant-based protein supplements outperform low or no protein but are generally less effective than whey or milk protein, citing a Bayesian meta-analysis. It describes the evidence for BCAAs on soreness and fatigue, and for bromelain, as inconclusive or mixed.
paper.limitations: The review has no quantitative synthesis and no structured appraisal, and the study selection is not reproducible from the text. Its own appendix notes short follow-up, small and non-randomised samples, self-reported intake, and few analyses by sex or age across the cited studies. Some statements go beyond the cited evidence, such as describing inflammation as a causal mechanism for recovery.
paper.practicalImplications: Build recovery nutrition on a balanced diet and use supplements where intake is insufficient, such as protein or electrolytes after high sweat losses. Choose third-party tested products, because the review notes that supplement labels can be inaccurate and some products contain unauthorized pharmaceuticals. Treat functional foods as complements to whole-food intake, not replacements for it.
paper.athleteDev: Use protein and carbohydrate intake after training to support repair and glycogen restoration, and note that strict timing matters less if daily needs are already met. The cited evidence suggests animal and plant protein sources differ in effectiveness, so check that total daily protein intake is adequate.
paper.rtp: This review does not evaluate return-to-sport or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot be used to set a rehabilitation nutrition protocol. Its mentions of injury risk rest on the mixed BCAA and omega-3 evidence it cites.

records.sourceFile: Fruit‑Derived Polyphenol Supplementation for Athlete Recovery and Performance.pdf

paper.citation: Bowtell J, Kelly V. Fruit-Derived Polyphenol Supplementation for Athlete Recovery and Performance. Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarizes evidence on fruit-derived polyphenol supplementation for exercise performance and recovery. The authors report that acute doses of about 300 mg polyphenols 1 to 2 hours before exercise may improve endurance and repeated-sprint performance, based on a small number of studies with methodological limitations. They also report that more than 1000 mg per day for 3 or more days before and after exercise is associated with better recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage, mainly through antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms.
paper.tldr: Acute doses of about 300 mg of fruit polyphenols before exercise may help endurance and repeated-sprint performance, but the evidence is small and mixed. The authors report a larger body of evidence that more than 1000 mg a day for 3 or more days helps recovery from muscle damage, much of it from Montmorency cherry trials.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal. The authors organize studies into acute and chronic performance trials and into recovery-from-muscle-damage trials, and summarize them in tables by population, dose, protocol and outcome. The review was published in a supplement supported by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute.
paper.findings: For performance, acute trials of pomegranate, cherry, cocoa and other extracts gave mixed results, with some showing better time to exhaustion or power output and others showing no difference, and chronic blackcurrant, grape and pomegranate studies also varied. For recovery, five of nine Montmorency cherry trials reported favorable effects on muscle function or performance, and those trials provided at least 1200 mg polyphenols per day, while soreness was reduced in half of eight cherry studies. Pomegranate trials mostly reported faster recovery of isometric strength but reduced soreness in only one study, and one blueberry trial reported faster recovery of knee extensor strength.
paper.limitations: The review has no search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. The authors note that polyphenol composition varies by batch, that most studies did not measure plasma phenolics, and that serum markers may not reflect processes inside muscle. The first author received an honorarium from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute for writing the review.
paper.practicalImplications: For an acute performance aim, the authors suggest about 300 mg polyphenols 1 to 2 hours before exercise. For recovery, they suggest more than 1000 mg per day for 3 or more days before and after heavy or repeated sessions, which they estimate 300 g of Montmorency cherries would provide. Check the polyphenol content of each product batch, since composition varies, and expect the clearest support for recovery of muscle function and soreness rather than for performance.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest polyphenols may help time-trial and repeated-sprint performance when taken 1 to 2 hours before competition or for 1 to 6 weeks beforehand, but they describe this as early evidence. They also suggest they may be considered during repeated-sprint or high-intensity interval training, while noting that a training benefit has not been demonstrated and that evidence in resistance training is lacking.
paper.rtp: The review covers recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage in trained or recreationally active adults, not injury or return to sport. It does not test rehabilitation after injury, so it should not be used for return-to-play or rehabilitation decisions.

records.sourceFile: Glutamine Supplementation - A Possible Strategy to Help Mitigate Health Risks of Heat-Related Illness.pdf

paper.citation: Zuhl M, Specht J, Beatty S, Mermier C. Glutamine Supplementation: A Possible Strategy to Help Mitigate Health Risks of Heat-Related Illness. Journal of Nutrition and Metabolism. 2024;2024:1638244.
paper.abstract: The authors review the literature on glutamine during heat stress and exertional heat illness. They cover intestinal barrier damage, immune and cytokine responses, antioxidant defence, hydration and fatigue, and conclude that glutamine may be a useful adjunct to cooling and work-rest strategies.
paper.tldr: This narrative review proposes that glutamine may help protect the gut, immune system and antioxidant defences during exertional heat stress. Most of the mechanistic support comes from animal and cell studies, and the human trials give mixed results.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, date range or selection criteria. It draws on animal, cell and human studies of glutamine during heat stress, together with surveillance reports of heat illness among workers, military personnel and athletes.
paper.findings: The review reports that 7 days of 0.90 g/kg/day glutamine, or a single 0.90 g/kg dose, prevented the rise in intestinal permeability after 60 min of high-intensity treadmill running in the heat in the authors' earlier work. A low dose of 0.30 g/kg/day did not change permeability or IFABP after about 22 min of exhaustive running in heat or 80 min of walking, and other human results are mixed: one 0.15 g/kg dose raised plasma total antioxidant capacity at 4 h after 78 min of heat stress, and a 0.60 g/kg dose before exercise in heat increased only T-lymphocyte mobilization. The review also cites a glutamine-enriched hydration mix that increased sodium and water absorption in healthy adults.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative with no described search or selection method, so its evidence base cannot be audited, and much of the cited human work is from the authors' own group. Most mechanistic evidence is from animal and cell models, and the human trials differ in dose, timing and sampling, which the review itself notes. The suggested 0.15 to 0.30 g/kg/day range is justified by raised plasma glutamine without adverse effects, is lower than the 0.90 g/kg doses behind the clearest gut-permeability results, and no cited study measured heat illness as an outcome.
paper.practicalImplications: Glutamine should not replace cooling, hydration, acclimation and work-rest measures, because no cited study shows that it prevents exertional heat illness. If staff consider it, the review's split doses before and after heat exposure, with large single boluses avoided because doses at or above 0.90 g/kg have been linked to GI discomfort, are the authors' own proposals based on plasma glutamine responses.
paper.athleteDev: Glutamine is not a substitute for heat acclimation, hydration and cooling in heat training. The human performance benefit is not established, since the review notes limited data suggesting improved performance.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport after heat illness, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. It concerns prevention and mechanisms, and does not show that glutamine speeds recovery from exertional heat illness.

records.sourceFile: High Prevalence of Cannabidiol Use Within Male Professional Rugby Union and League Players - A Quest for Pain Relief and Enhanced Recover.pdf

paper.citation: Kasper AM, Sparks SA, Hooks M, Skeer M, Webb B, Nia H, et al. High prevalence of cannabidiol use within male professional rugby union and league players: a quest for pain relief and enhanced recovery. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: An anonymous online survey of 517 male professional rugby union and league players found that 26% had used or were still using cannabidiol (CBD). Use was higher in union than league and rose with age, with the main reasons given being pain relief, recovery and sleep. The authors call for player education on CBD risks and for research on its efficacy.
paper.tldr: About a quarter of professional rugby players surveyed had used CBD, mainly for recovery, pain and sleep, and use was highest in older players. Players most often perceived a sleep benefit, and the study did not test whether CBD works or whether products contained THC.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional anonymous online survey of 15 multiple-choice questions, sent to professional male players from 30 invited teams (English Premiership, Pro14 and Super League) in the 2019 to 2020 season, with 25 teams responding. Responses were coded in Excel and analysed with goodness-of-fit and independence chi-square tests, Cramer's V, Bonferroni post hoc tests, and Kruskal-Wallis tests for team differences.
paper.findings: Of 517 respondents, 91% (472) were aware of CBD and 133 had used it, reported as 26% (8% current, 18% previous). Use was higher in union than league (chi-square 8.29, p = .004), did not differ by position (p = .760) and differed by age (p < .001), with fewer users than expected aged 18 to 23 and more aged over 28; team-level use ranged from 5% to 70%. Users cited recovery or pain (80%) and sleep (78%), 67% perceived a benefit (sleep 41%, recovery or pain 14%), no adverse effects were reported, and 79% believed their product was batch tested although only one listed product appeared to be.
paper.limitations: The survey is self-reported and anonymous, products were not tested and the authors note perceived benefits may be placebo. Figures are inconsistent: the abstract reports 41% use in players 28 and older and 68% perceived benefit, while the Discussion gives 39% ("almost 40%") and 67%; the 26% use rate is described as a share of the 472 aware players, but 133 users is 26% of all 517 respondents and 28% of 472. The abstract attributes the information sources (Internet 73%, teammate 61%, nutritionist 16%) to CBD users, while the Results report them for all 472 aware players.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should ask players directly about CBD, since few players reported getting information from a nutritionist (16%) or other staff (4%). The authors call for education on anti-doping risk and product quality, because THC may exceed legal thresholds in some products and most users wrongly assumed their product was batch tested. The reported benefits should not be treated as evidence of effect.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to training prescription. The study does not test performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study does not test pain or recovery outcomes after injury, so it cannot inform return to play.

records.sourceFile: High protein plant-based diet vs a protein-matched omnivorous diet to support resistance training adaptations - A comparison between habitual vegans and omnivores.pdf

paper.citation: Hevia-Larraín V, Gualano B, Longobardi I, Gil S, Fernandes AL, Costa LAR, et al. High-Protein Plant-Based Diet Versus a Protein-Matched Omnivorous Diet to Support Resistance Training Adaptations: A Comparison Between Habitual Vegans and Omnivores. Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: Nineteen habitual vegans and 19 omnivores (untrained young men) completed a 12-week supervised lower-limb resistance training program. Habitual protein was adjusted to 1.6 g/kg/day with soy (vegans) or whey (omnivores). Leg lean mass, muscle and fiber cross-sectional area, and leg-press 1RM rose in both groups with no between-group differences.
paper.tldr: Untrained vegan and omnivorous young men gained similar muscle size and strength over 12 weeks of leg training when both reached about 1.6 g protein/kg/day. The vegan group needed large soy protein supplements to get there, so the result does not show that plant foods alone would perform the same way.
paper.methods: Non-randomized parallel-group study: 19 habitual vegans and 19 omnivores completed twice-weekly supervised leg-press and leg-extension training for 12 weeks. Protein was topped up to 1.6 g/kg/day with soy (vegans) or whey (omnivores) supplements, and outcomes were DXA leg lean mass, ultrasound muscle cross-sectional area, muscle biopsy fiber area (11 per group), and leg-press 1RM, analyzed with mixed models. The power calculation required 17 per group, and 23 per group were targeted to allow for dropouts.
paper.findings: Both groups increased leg lean mass by 1.2 kg (vegans 18.9 to 20.1 kg; omnivores 19.1 to 20.3 kg), with no group difference in change (p = 0.99). Vastus lateralis area rose by 2.2 cm2 in vegans and 2.8 cm2 in omnivores, and leg-press 1RM rose from 258 to 354 kg (vegans) and 261 to 383 kg (omnivores), with no group-by-time interaction (p = 0.10). Type I and type II fiber areas increased in both groups, with no group-by-time interaction.
paper.limitations: Groups were self-selected by habitual diet, not randomized, the trial was registered retrospectively, fiber data come from 11 per group, dietary intake relied on 24-h recalls, and physical activity was not reassessed at the end. The abstract and results disagree: the abstract gives 1RM changes of 97 and 117 kg and an omnivore rectus femoris change of 0.9 cm2, while the reported pre and post values give 96 and 122 kg and 0.7 cm2, and the results values are used here. Baseline leg lean mass for vegans is 18.1 kg in Table 1 but 18.9 kg in the text, and the discussion gives omnivore supplement intake as about 41 g/day versus 39 g/day in the results.
paper.practicalImplications: For untrained young adults doing resistance training, a vegan diet providing about 1.6 g protein/kg/day produced muscle and strength gains similar to a protein-matched mixed diet over 12 weeks. Achieving that target required about 58 g/day of supplemental soy protein in the vegan group compared with about 39 g/day of whey in the omnivore group, so staff should plan for the extra protein and not assume a food-only vegan plan would match these results.
paper.athleteDev: In untrained young men, protein source did not change 12-week gains in muscle size or leg strength when total protein was about 1.6 g/kg/day, which supports a plant-based diet for these adults only if protein intake is actively managed. The study did not test trained athletes, women, or whole-food-only diets.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It involved healthy untrained men and measured no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.
